title: ahol and amikor: Relative Clauses of Place and Time

sections.content: 'aki' and 'amely' cover people and things, but a church-and-state topic also needs to name places (a monastery) and times (a year, an event). Hungarian has two more relative words for exactly this: 'ahol' ('where', pointing back to a place already named) and 'amikor' ('when', pointing back to a time or event already named). They work just like 'aki' and 'amely' — they refer back to something already in the sentence and introduce extra information about it — but, being adverbs rather than pronouns, they never take case endings.

sections.title: Relative adverbs
rows: where (referring to a place already named)
when (referring to a time or event already named)

items.spanish: Pannonhalma, ahol Szent István idejében bencés szerzetesek éltek, ma is működő kolostor.
items.english: Pannonhalma, where Benedictine monks lived in Saint István's time, is still a working monastery today.

items.spanish: 1083-ban, amikor Szent Lászlót és Szent Imrét is szentté avatták, az egész ország ünnepelt.
items.english: In 1083, when Saint László and Saint Imre were also canonized, the whole country celebrated.

items.spanish: Az egyházmegyék azokban a városokban jöttek létre, ahol püspöki székhelyeket alapítottak.
items.english: Dioceses were established in those towns where episcopal seats were founded.

sections.content: You now have a full family of relative words: aki/akik for people, amely/amelyek for things, ahol for places, amikor for times. Pick the one that matches what the antecedent actually is, and remember that only aki takes case endings (akit, akinek) — ahol and amikor stay in this one form no matter what role they play in their own clause.
